Does Women's Body Appreciation Differ by Sexual Orientation? A Brief Report
School of Social Welfare, The University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas, USA
Center for Health Promotion, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, Massachusetts, USA

Department of Health, Human Performance and Recreation, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Arkansas, USA; The Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender and Reproduction, Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana, USA

Sexual minority identification may affect women's experiences of body image; however, existing research has solely compared lesbian and heterosexual women. The purpose of this exploratory study is to examine differences in body appreciation among women who identify as heterosexual, bisexual, and other sexual minorities were found. Findings from analysis of covariance revealed significant differences in body appreciation between sexual minority and heterosexual women while controlling for demographic characteristics, and no significant differences in body appreciation between bisexual women and other sexual minority women were found. Findings suggest body appreciation may be affected by sexual orientation, but further research with more diverse samples is warranted.
KEYWORDS body image, sexual orientation, women
A woman's sexual orientation is one aspect of her identity that may intersect with her body image (T. Morrison & McCutcheon, 2012). In particular, a
Address correspondence to Virginia Ramseyer Winter, BSW, MSW, The University of Kansas, School of Social Welfare, 1545 Lilac Lane, Lawrence, KS 66045, USA. E-mail: ginnywinter@ku.edu

woman's body image may be affected by the aesthetic expectations of her specific sexual subculture to produce differential levels of body satisfaction, evaluation, and salience (Heffernan, 1996; T. Morrison & McCutcheon, 2012). Existing empirical literature on the differences between groups of women who vary by sexual orientation primarily focus on comparing lesbian women to heterosexual women, thereby leaving out other groups of sexual minority women such as bisexual and queer-identified women. Additionally, as with much of the body image literature, these studies tend to measure levels of body image dissatisfaction and pathology, leaving the exploration of resilience to sexual objectification and body-related appreciation underrepresented (Wood-Barcalow, Tylka, & Augustus-Horvath, 2010). This research report focuses on the potential relationships between sexual orientation and body appreciation, a multifaceted measure of positive body appraisal and evaluation, in a sample of adult women.

Research comparing body images of lesbian and heterosexual women are inconsistent; some researchers report significant differences in body image (Owens, Hughes, & Owens-Nicholson, 2002; Share & Mintz, 2002) whereas others report null findings (Beren, Hayden, Wilfley, & Grilo, 1996). For example, Share and Mintz (2002) found that lesbian women had significantly higher levels of body esteem than heterosexual women. Similarly, Owens et al. (2002) reported that lesbian women had more positive body image and fewer negative attitudes about weight and eating compared to heterosexual women. Conversely, Beren et al. (1996) found that lesbian and heterosexual women's body dissatisfaction did not differ significantly. Peplau et al. (2009) also reported that lesbian women were less concerned about being overweight than their heterosexual counterparts and, despite having a significantly higher Body Mass Index (BMI), lesbian women did not significantly differ from heterosexuals in regard to body satisfaction.

A meta-analysis provides some clarity on the relationship between women's body image and their sexual orientation. M. Morrison, Morrison, and Sager (2004) conducted a meta-analysis on 32 studies that measured body satisfaction/dissatisfaction and compared heterosexual women to lesbian women and heterosexual men to gay men. They found body satisfaction did not differ significantly between lesbian and heterosexual women. However, among a small number of studies (k = 4) in which lesbian and heterosexual women reported comparable weights, lesbian women had slightly higher body satisfaction than their heterosexual counterparts (M. Morrison et al., 2004). Thus, when body weight is accounted for, it appears lesbian women report better body image than heterosexual women. Similarly, Alvy (2013) found that lesbian women reported lower body dissatisfaction as well as a larger ideal body size.

This meta-analysis specifically focused on studies comparing lesbianidentified and heterosexually-identified women, thereby eliding the potential contribution of bisexual or queer-identified women, whose body image may

be different than lesbian-identified women (T. Morrison & McCutcheon, 2012). Bisexual or queer-identified women may be similarly ensconced in nonheterosexual subcultures as well as potentially heterosexual subcultures. In a qualitative study exploring body image among lesbian and bisexual women, Huxley, Clarke, and Halliwell (2011) found that women who had experienced relationships with men had beauty practices and body-related behaviors that were influenced by their concern with men's opinions of them. The authors concluded that bisexually-identified women may experience pressure related to appearance in a unique way. In another qualitative study, researchers found that bisexual women expressed the desire to obtain the beauty and thin standards of the mainstream culture much as heterosexual women do, but the bisexual women in the study also expressed conflict between their desire to reject these standards and simultaneously live up to them (Chmielewski & Yost, 2013). Thus, bisexual women may experience body image differently from lesbian and heterosexual women, and including a more diverse sample of sexual minority women in comparisons regarding body image will provide a more comprehensive understanding of these issues.

All of the aforementioned studies of body image comparisons by sexual orientation include the evaluative, or satisfaction/dissatisfaction dimensions of body image, accounting less for the multidimensionality of the construct. Body appreciation, a more recently conceptualized measure of body image, goes beyond body evaluation to include respect for one's body, acceptance of one's body, favorable opinions of one's body, and the ability to reject unrealistic cultural expectations of women's bodies and appearance (Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005). Given that sexual minority women may place differential emphasis on the function and ability of one's body, as opposed to just its appearance (Heffernan, 1996), body appreciation differences may better capture differences between sexual orientation groups. We tested two hypotheses: (1) body appreciation would be higher for sexual minority women than heterosexually-identified women when controlling for age, BMI, sexual relationship status, and education level; and (2) body appreciation would be lower for bisexual women than other sexual minority women when controlling for sexual relationship status.

This study includes data from two samples, one collected in 2010 (Sample 1) and the other collected in 2012 (Sample 2), with no overlapping data between the two studies. Of the 1,152 women who participated, only those who completed the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) were included in the analyses (n = 1,009). Outliers were identified by examining boxplots and

conducting Mahalanobis tests. Women age 50 years and older and women with a BMI greater than 46 or less than 15 were excluded from all analyses. This resulted in a final sample size of 903 women. We utilized listwise deletion for missing data in all analyses (Saunders et al., 2006).

We conducted ANOVA and chi-square analyses to determine if there were significant differences between the women who completed the BAS and those who did not. We found that those who did not complete the BAS were approximately 1\frac{1}{2} years older but were not significantly different by BMI, sexual orientation, education level, race, or sexual relationship status.

We conducted ANOVA and chi-square analyses to determine if there were significant differences between the women in the two samples. We found that the two samples did not differ significantly based on race or sexual orientation. The women from Sample 1 were more likely to be in a sexual relationship with more than one sexual partner (20.1% for Sample 1 and 11% for Sample 2), have a bachelor's degree or higher (83.7% for Sample 1 and 55.5% for Sample 2), have a higher BMI (M BMI for Sample 1 = 27.78; M BMI for Sample 2 = 25.46), and be older (M age for Sample 1 = 28.9; M age for Sample 2 = 27.01).
The majority of the sample was White (86.3%) and the sample was highly educated, with 67.1% holding a bachelor degree or higher. See Table 1 for

Body appreciation. The Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos et al., 2005), a 13-item scale with response options of 1 (never) to 5 (always). Sample items include "I am attentive to my body's needs" and "I feel good about my body." The responses were averaged to compute a BAS score for each participant, with a higher BAS score reflecting higher body appreciation. Avalos et al. (2005) measured test–retest reliability with a sample of college women over a 3-week period and found that the scale score reliability of the BAS was high (Cronbach's \alpha = .91 to .93). The scale score reliability of BAS scores in this sample is estimated to be high (Cronbach's \alpha = .92, confidence interval [CI] [.92, .93]). The mean BAS score for the current sample was 3.64 (SD = 0.69). BAS score was slightly negatively skewed and did not require variable transformation.

Sexual orientation. Sexual orientation was collected using a self-reported, open-ended question, "What words do you use to describe your sexual orientation?" for Study 1 and a similar question for Study 2, "What is your sexual orientation?" For the purposes of this study, responses were categorized into either sexual minority identity (i.e., lesbian, bisexual, queer, other) or heterosexual identity. The majority of the sample identified as heterosexual (69.5%) whereas bisexual-identified participants made up the majority of the sexual minority group (n = 131, 14.5%). Due to the small sample size of lesbian-, queer-, and other-identified women, the sample was put into two groups: sexual minority women and heterosexual women for the first set of analyses. For the second set of analyses, heterosexual women were excluded and the sample was put into two groups: bisexually-identified women and women who identify as another sexual minority.
Body Mass Index. Participants self-reported weight and height. BMI was computed from these variables. The mean BMI for the sample was 26.24 (SD = 6.80).
Sexual relationship status. Sexual relationship status was collected with the following item, "Are you currently in a sexual relationship?" Response

options include: "I am in an exclusive/monogamous sexual relationship" (i.e., sexual activity only with each other); "I am having sexual relationships with more than one person"; "I am sexually active, but don't consider myself to be in a 'sexual relationship"; "I am currently not sexually active with another person"; and no response. This variable was collapsed into three categories: exclusive/monogamous sexual relationship, sexual relationship with more than one person, and not currently in a defined sexual relationship. The majority of participants reported being in an exclusive/monogamous sexual relationship (59.5%).

For both studies data collection and recruitment mechanisms were very similar. A detailed description of study procedures can be found elsewhere for Sample 1 (Satinsky, Reece, Dennis, Sanders, & Bardzell, 2012) and Sample 2 (Satinsky & Jozkowski, in press). In brief, data were collected online using Qualtrics and participants were recruited through social media websites and e-mail list serves. Recruitment messages included a brief description of the study with a link to the study website. Interested women were instructed to click on the link that directed them to the study website where they could read more information about the study and what was expected of them if they participated. Interested individuals were instructed to click to the next page that provided a study information sheet. The study information sheet gave additional information about the study and notified individuals that by participating in the study, they were indicating their consent. As such, no contact information was obtained from participants, to maintain anonymity.

The inclusion criteria for both studies were that potential participants identified as women and were over the age of 18. Institutional Review Board approval was obtained prior to data collection for both studies.

Bivariate analyses. To determine which participant characteristics may confound the relationship between body appreciation and sexual orientation for heterosexual and sexual minority women, we ran ANOVA and chi-square analyses. Sexual minority participants were 2 years older (M=29.17) than heterosexual participants (M=27.17), F(1,868)=14.49, p<.001, \eta^2=.016. Sexual minority participants also reported larger body size, as measured by BMI (M BMI = 27.56) than heterosexual participants (M BMI = 25.61), F(1,733)=12.93, p<.001, \eta^2=.017. There were also significant differences in

the sexual relationship status of sexual minority and heterosexual participant, \chi^2(2, N=872)=201.61, p<.001, \phi=.481, with nonheterosexual participants being less likely to be in a monogamous relationship, more likely to be in a sexual relationship with more than one person, and less likely to be sexually active but not define it as a "sexual relationship." Sexual minority participants were more likely to have a bachelor's degree or higher than heterosexual participants, \chi^2(1, N=865)=7.38, p<.01, \phi=.092. Given the statistically significant differences in age, BMI, sexual relationship status, and education level between sexual minority and heterosexual participants, these variables were controlled for when conducting the analysis of covariance (ANCOVA).

ANCOVA. To determine if BAS score differed significantly based on sexual orientation, we conducted an ANCOVA, controlling for the variables mentioned above. All assumptions required for an ANCOVA were met. Results indicated there was a statistically significant difference in BAS score for sexual orientation while holding age, BMI, sexual relationship status, and education level constant, F(1, 724) = 8.66, p < .001, partial \eta^2 = .012. Thus, sexual minority women (adjusted M = 3.77) differed significantly in body appreciation from heterosexual women (adjusted M = 3.60) and sexual orientation accounted for approximately 1.2% of the variance. BMI was the only other variable significantly related to BAS, F(1, 724) = 46.84, p < .001, partial \eta^2 = .061, and accounted for 6.1% of the variance.

Bivariate analyses. To determine the confounding variables in the relationship between sexual orientation and body appreciation among bisexual and other sexual minority women, we ran ANOVA and chi-square analyses. There were no significant differences between bisexual and other sexual minority participants by age, F(1, 263) = 1.20, p = .274, \eta^2 = .016; BMI, F(1, 225) = 0.109, p = .742 \eta^2 = .017; or education, \chi^2(1, N = 265) = .20, p = .655, \phi = .027. Bisexual and other sexual minority participants significantly differed by sexual relationship status, \chi^2(1, N = 266) = 94.77, p < .001, \phi = .597, with bisexual women being less likely to be in a monogamous/exclusive sexual relationship and more likely to be in a sexual relationship with more than one person. Given the significant difference in sexual relationship status, we controlled for this variable when conducting the ANCOVA.

ANCOVA. To determine if BAS score differed significantly for bisexual women and other sexual minority women, we ran an ANCOVA, controlling for sexual relationship status. All assumptions for the ANCOVA were met. Results indicated there were no significant differences in BAS score for bisexual and other sexual minority women while holding sexual relationship

status constant, F(1, 265) = 0.305, p = .581, partial \eta^2 = .001. Thus, bisexual women (adjusted M = 3.73) did not differ significantly in body appreciation from other sexual minority women (adjusted M = 3.69).

This research report adds to the existing body of literature in two ways: by including sexual minority women of various identifications, not just lesbian women; and by offering initial information on the levels of body appreciation in an understudied group of women. Body appreciation as a construct offers an alternate and more holistic means of measuring aspects of body image that could be especially salient to sexual minority communities who may have differing aesthetic bodily norms. In addition, as the field of body image research moves away from a pathologizing perspective to one based on strengths and resilience (Tylka, 2011), data on why women from stigmatized sexual communities are still reporting equal or higher levels of body appreciation may offer insight on potential sites of resistance to and resilience from damaging hegemonic body norms.

Objectification theory is often used in existing literature to explain two conflicting outcomes: why lesbian women report better body image than heterosexual women and why there might be no reported difference in body image between lesbian and heterosexual women. Objectification theory posits that within Western cultures, women's bodies are treated as objects available for the pleasure of and for consumption by men. Culturallevel objectification leads to self-objectification, "The tendency to introject an objectifying third-person perspective on one's own body, evaluating it in terms of its value and attractiveness to others, rather than its value and function for the self" (Fredrickson, Hendler, Nilsen, O'Barr, & Roberts, 2011, p. 690), which causes body shame (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997). Studies that find significantly better body image among nonheterosexual women suggest that these women "do not think of themselves as objects to be defined by male subjects" (Dworkin, 1989, p. 28) and that lesbian subculture has different and more flexible body norms, which may affect body image (Alvy, 2013). Thus, according to this argument, because nonheterosexual women are not subjected to cultural objectification at the same level as heterosexually-identified women, nonheterosexual women may not experience the same consequences of that objectification.

Conversely, studies that do not find significant differences in body image by sexual orientation argue that gender has greater implications for body image than sexual orientation; all women are subjected to an objectifying culture and sexual orientation does not buffer this experience.
Our findings align with both of these arguments. It is notable that in our analyses, sexual minority women reported a higher mean body size and

more appreciation for their bodies, though the effect size was very small. Additionally, the correlation between BMI and BAS is stronger for heterosexual women than for sexual minority women in this sample. However, using Fisher's r-to-z transformation, we found that the association between weight and body appreciation is not stronger for heterosexual women (z=.41, p=.34). Therefore, the argument that the link between body size and body appreciation may be less relevant to sexual minority women, potentially because of less exposure to cultural-level objectification, is not supported in our sample. However, we did find support for Hypothesis 1 and the ANCOVA results for differences in BAS score between heterosexual and nonheterosexual women produced a very small effect size (\eta^2=.012). Given that we grouped all sexual minority women together, it is possible that identifying with different nonheterosexual orientations may yield different results. Therefore, we conducted an additional set of analyses to compare bisexual and other sexual minority women.

Again drawing from objectification theory, we hypothesized that bisexual women would have lower BAS scores than other sexual minority women due to being subjected to the male gaze via potential relationships with men (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997). Our analyses did not support Hypothesis 2. In fact, bisexual women's body appreciation scores did not significantly differ from other sexual minority women's scores. Thus, body appreciation does not differ by sexual orientation among this sample of sexual minority-identified women.

It is possible that women in same-sex relationships engage in partner objectification by comparing themselves to each other (Huxley et al., 2011) in a similar way that bisexual women in relationships with men may be objectified by the male gaze, as is proposed by objectification theory (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997). Although women in same-sex relationships may be less subject to an objectifying male gaze from female intimate partners, a more body-positive lesbian culture (Alvy, 2013) may not protect them from idealized mainstream images or from self-objectification. Accordingly, our results suggest that the prevalent focus on a thin body type in heterosexually oriented society may infiltrate potential body-positive narratives in sexual subcultures.

The lack of significance in our results comparing bisexual women to women who identify as other sexual minorities may be due to missing key variables in our analyses. In an exploratory qualitative study of bisexual and lesbian body image, Leavy and Hastings (2010) reported that bisexual participants described different degrees of pressure to conform to mainstream ideal body types depending on the gender of their current dating partner. Chmielewski and Yost (2013) also found that involvement in the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender community, feminist identity, and sexual prejudice were important confounders in the relationship between bisexual identity and body image. Future research should include these ad-
ditional confounders when exploring these relationships among bisexual women.

There are several limitations of this study. The study is comprised of primarily educated White women, limiting the generalizability of the results to various communities of color or to women of lower educational or socioeconomic status. Furthermore, due to a technical error in data collection of one study that resulted in high missing data, we were unable to include race/ethnicity in our analyses. Data from each sample were collected crosssectionally, and the two samples were collected at two different points in time which limits our ability to infer causality. However, sexual orientation and BAS were assessed at the same time point. Additionally, sexual orientation is dichotomized for this study, reducing variability. It is possible that variability in sexual orientation may be important in this area of scholarship (Leavy & Hastings, 2010). Future studies could address these limitations by utilizing a more ethnically and educationally diverse sample of women, collecting data longitudinally, as well as assessing participants' perceptions of body ideals specific to their sexual subcultures and experiences of minority stress (Alvy, 2013) as a means of better understanding why sexual orientation might affect body image reports.

Given that body image in all its forms is directly connected to health outcomes such as depression (Atlantis & Ball, 2008) and risky sexual behaviors (Ramseyer Winter & Satinsky, 2014) among others, it is imperative to continue conducting research on the ways in which a woman's various aspects of her identity, including sexual orientation, may affect her body image. If sexual minority women report higher levels of body appreciation than heterosexually-identified women, there are lessons to be learned from these communities regarding means of buffering objectification that could have implications for interventions promoting body appreciation in women. To better answer how body appreciation among sexual minority women varies and compares, researchers must purposively sample women of intersecting sexual and racial identities, to further elucidate potential differences between and within groups of women, with the goal of creating culturally competent means of improving body image for all.

Virginia Ramseyer Winter, MSW, is a PhD candidate in the School of Social Welfare at the University of Kansas. Her research focuses on the implications of body image on women's physical, mental, and sexual health.

Sonya Satinsky, PhD, MPH, is the director of the Center for Health Promotion at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. Her research focuses on the intersections and interplay of body shape, size and image, sexual health and sexual behavior, and gender, race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation.

Kristen N. Jozkowski, PhD, is an assistant professor of health promotion and affiliate faculty in gender studies at the University of Arkansas. She is also a Research Fellow at The Kinsey Institute for Research in Sex, Gender and Reproduction. Dr. Jozkowski earned her PhD in health behavior from Indiana University. Her research focuses on women's sexuality broadly with specific focuses in sexual consent and sexual function.
